title: The Days of My Life Have Been Few and Evil — Meeting the King, Buying Grain, a Burying Place
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. I want to open this lesson with a very simple question: if somebody asked you, "How has your life gone?" — how would you answer?
Most of us would answer politely: oh, not too bad, thank the Lord. And inside a church we are even more likely to say it that way.

In Genesis chapter 47, a man of a hundred and thirty is standing in front of Pharaoh. And Pharaoh asks him, "How old are you?" — the Hebrew is literally, "How many are the days of the years of your life?"
He answers, "The days of the years of my life have been few and evil. They have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their pilgrimage."
Few and evil. That is one of the most honest pieces of self-description in the whole Bible. And yet only a verse earlier, he had just finished blessing Pharaoh.
"From among his brothers he took five men, and presented them to Pharaoh." (Genesis 47:2)

Look first at the arrangement. Joseph had coached them on how to answer, and they said exactly what he had told them to say: "Your servants are shepherds, both we, and our fathers … Now therefore, please let your servants dwell in the land of Goshen."
What they asked for was not a palace but a pasture. The Hebrew is מִרְעֶה (*mireh*) — grazing land.
Pharaoh not only granted it; he added a sentence of his own: "If you know any able men among them, then put them in charge of my livestock."
"Able men" is אַנְשֵׁי־חַיִל (*anshei-chayil*), "men of capability, men of strength" — and it is exactly the phrase Moses would later use when he chose out officials over Israel.
Brothers and sisters, there is something lovely here: shepherding was a despised trade in Egypt, and yet that very same trade, in Pharaoh's mouth, has just turned into an appointment.
That one skill of yours that people look down on — God has ways of turning it, in the right place, into an office.
And then comes the first summit of the chapter:
"Joseph brought in Jacob, his father, and set him before Pharaoh; and Jacob blessed Pharaoh." (Genesis 47:7)
"Blessed" is וַיְבָרֶךְ (*vayvarech*). And at the end of verse 10 it is said all over again: "Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and went out from the presence of Pharaoh."
One at the front, one at the back — two blessings.

Look hard at this picture. An old shepherd of a hundred and thirty. A refugee. A man who has just fled a famine in Canaan and who eats only because of his son's connections. He is standing in front of the most powerful monarch in the world of his day — and then he blesses that monarch.
Hebrews chapter 7 says, "But without any dispute the lesser is blessed by the greater."

In human eyes, Pharaoh is the great one and Jacob is the small one. In God's eyes the order runs the other way round — because back in chapter 12 God had said to Abraham, "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you."
Jacob had nothing at all in his hands. But he had that promise in his hands.
Brothers and sisters, let me spell one thing out very carefully: standing here means the office of carrying a promise; it does not mean being a superior kind of person.
Jacob did not think himself a cut above anybody. He knew that he was holding something nobody else was holding — and that the something was meant to be given away.

Our identity is not defined by our circumstances. You may be the person in your company with the least say, the one in your family who is valued least, the newest face in your church — but if you are in Christ, then you are holding a blessing you can hand to somebody.
To establish God's system is to walk into any room at all carrying the blessing God has given you.
A refugee blessing a king — is that the right way round?

Hebrews chapter 7 says, "But without any dispute the lesser is blessed by the greater." In human eyes Pharaoh is the great one and Jacob is the small one; in God's eyes the order runs the other way round, because back in chapter 12 God had said to Abraham, "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you." Jacob had nothing at all in his hands, but he had that promise in his hands. And here is what has to be spelled out carefully: standing means the office of carrying a promise, not a superior kind of status. He did not think himself a cut above anybody. He knew that he was holding something nobody else was holding — and that the something was meant to be given away.
Is a skill that people look down on worth anything at all?

Look at the way this chapter arranges it. Shepherding was a despised trade in Egypt, so what the brothers asked for was not a palace but a pasture — the Hebrew word means grazing land. And Pharaoh not only granted it; he added a sentence of his own: "If you know any able men among them, then put them in charge of my livestock." That phrase "able men" is, in Hebrew, "men of capability, men of strength" — the very phrase Moses would later use when he chose out officials over Israel. The same trade: looked down on in one place, an appointment in another. That one skill of yours that people look down on — God has ways of turning it, in the right place, into an office. What you have to do is to do it well first.
2. A Light from the Original: Few and Evil
Then Pharaoh asks a very deliberate, very formal question: "How old are you?"
The Hebrew is יְמֵי שְׁנֵי חַיֶּיךָ (*yemei shenei chayecha*), literally "the days of the years of your life" — a very formal and very respectful way of asking.
And Jacob's answer — I want you to listen to it one word at a time:

"The years of my pilgrimage are one hundred thirty years. The days of the years of my life have been few and evil. They have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their pilgrimage." (Genesis 47:9)

First: he does not say "I have lived." He says "I have sojourned." The Hebrew is מְגוּרַי (*megurai*) — my days as a stranger passing through. In the last stretch of his life he still calls himself a sojourner.
Second: "few and evil" is מְעַט וְרָעִים (*me'at vera'im*), literally "few, and they have been bad."
A hundred and thirty years, and he calls that "few"? Yes. Set beside Abraham's hundred and seventy-five and Isaac's hundred and eighty, it felt short to him.

And as for "bad" — look at the life. Twenty years on the run. An uncle who cheated him over a marriage and made him work it off twice. The wife he loved most dying in childbirth by the roadside. A daughter violated. Sons who put a city to the sword. A firstborn who defiled his concubine. The son he loved best "devoured by an animal" for twenty-two years. And now a famine has driven him into a foreign country.
He says it was bad. He is not wrong.
Brothers and sisters, I want to stop here and say something that matters a great deal.
Some people read this far and say: Jacob is being far too negative; talking like that does not sound like faith.

But notice: God does not rebuke him. The text does not add one word of comment. And immediately afterwards, in verse 10, he blesses Pharaoh a second time — having said how bitter it had been, he goes on and blesses all the same.
More than half of the Psalms are laments. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" was written by David, and it is the line the Lord Jesus quoted on the cross.
Here is what honesty means: calling the bitter thing bitter, and not wrapping it up in spiritual language — because the One you are speaking to can take it.

Saying your own pain out loud is not unbelief; it is the evidence that the relationship is still alive. A person who is unfailingly polite with you and never says anything but the correct thing is usually not the person closest to you.
And notice one more thing: two things are present in this passage at the same time — he admits his own bitterness, and he still blesses other people.
That is a very mature life. An immature life can only pick one of the two: either pretend nothing is wrong and press the pain down, or be swallowed by the pain and be no blessing to anybody.
Honest on the one hand, giving on the other — this was the last lesson of Jacob's life, and he learned it.
"Few and evil" — is that not too negative, a sign of weak faith?

God does not rebuke him, and the text does not add one word of comment. And immediately afterwards, in verse 10, he blesses Pharaoh a second time — having said how bitter it had been, he goes on and blesses all the same. More than half of the Psalms are laments; "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" was written by David, and it is the line the Lord Jesus quoted on the cross. Here is what honesty means: calling the bitter thing bitter, and not wrapping it up in spiritual language — because the One you are speaking to can take it. Saying your own pain out loud is not unbelief; it is the evidence that the relationship is still alive — a person who never says anything to you but the correct thing is usually not the person closest to you.
He says "the years of my pilgrimage." What does that choice of word carry?

He does not say "I have lived"; he says "I have sojourned" — the Hebrew is "my days as a stranger passing through." A man of a hundred and thirty, in the last stretch of his life, still calls himself a sojourner. Hebrews chapter 11 describes the patriarchs in exactly those terms: "having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth", desiring a better country. That self-understanding matters enormously, because it decides how you look at everything in your hands: a traveller does not treat the inn as home, and so he does not lose his soul over the size of the room. And it also explains why, right at the end, he insisted on not being buried in Egypt.
From verse 13 the text turns to a passage that a great many people have no idea how to preach:

The famine grows heavier and heavier; Egypt and Canaan "fainted by reason of the famine." The people bought grain with their silver, and then the silver ran out — the Hebrew is אָפֵס (*afes*), "it came to zero."
They said, "Give us bread, for why should we die in your presence? For our money fails." Joseph said, "Give me your livestock; and I will give you food for your livestock, if your money is gone."
The next year the livestock was gone as well. And they said:

"We will not hide from my lord how our money is all spent, and the herds of livestock are my lord's. There is nothing left in the sight of my lord, but our bodies, and our lands. Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land for bread, and we and our land will be servants to Pharaoh." (Genesis 47:18–19)
"We will not hide" is לֹא־נְכַחֵד (*lo-nechached*) — that is how people talk when they have run out of road.
And notice one thing in particular: this proposal came from the people themselves. The text says it perfectly plainly: "Buy us and our land for bread."
And then they go straight on: "Give us seed, that we may live, and not die, and that the land won't be desolate."
Bread is today; seed is tomorrow. What they asked for was not only that they should not go hungry today, but that they should still be able to sow next year.
So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh — and then he said something rather remarkable:

"Behold, here is seed for you, and you shall sow the land." — the Hebrew is הֵא־לָכֶם זֶרַע (*he-lachem zera*), and that little word for "here, take it" occurs only this once in the whole Old Testament.

Then he lays down the rule: "It will happen at the harvests, that you shall give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four parts will be your own, for seed of the field, for your food, for them of your households, and for food for your little ones."
A fifth to Pharaoh, four fifths left with the people. And in verse 25, here is how the people react:
"You have saved our lives! Let us find favor in the sight of my lord, and we will be Pharaoh's servants."
"You have saved our lives" is הֶחֱיִתָנוּ (*hecheyitanu*) — "you have made us live" — from the same root as "to preserve life" back in chapter 45.
They are not complaining. They are giving thanks.
Brothers and sisters, there are two things I want to make plain here.

First, this passage is narrative, not norm. That the Bible records what Joseph did is not the same thing as the Bible teaching us what sort of economic system we ought to have. To take this passage and use it to support or to attack any modern economic argument is a misuse of it. The pulpit is not the place for political commentary.

Second, what this passage really wants us to see is the deepest question underneath it all: when the silver goes to zero, the livestock goes to zero and the land goes to zero — what is a human being left with?
The people said, "There is nothing left in the sight of my lord, but our bodies, and our lands."

And then the text says, right on the heels of it, in verse 27: "Israel lived in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen; and they got themselves possessions therein, and were fruitful, and multiplied exceedingly."
"Were fruitful, and multiplied" is וַיִּפְרוּ וַיִּרְבּוּ (*vayifru vayirbu*) — the very words of God's first blessing on humanity back in Genesis chapter 1.
While the whole of Egypt is selling its land and selling itself, God's people are being fruitful and multiplying. One and the same famine — two entirely different pictures.
Not because they were cleverer. Because the promise of God was on them.
The passage where Joseph buys the land and the people — how do you read it without misusing it?

There are two things that have to be made plain. First, this passage is narrative, not norm. That the Bible records what Joseph did is not the same thing as the Bible teaching us what sort of economic system we ought to have; to take it and use it to support or to attack any modern economic argument is a misuse of it. Second, we have to see what the text itself puts the weight on: this proposal came from the people themselves, and what they asked for was not only bread but seed as well — bread is today, seed is tomorrow. Joseph gave them the seed, and he set the tax at a fifth, leaving four fifths with the people; and the people's own reaction was, "You have saved our lives!"
One and the same famine — why two different pictures?

The whole of Egypt is selling its land and selling itself, and then verse 27 says: "Israel lived in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen; and they got themselves possessions therein, and were fruitful, and multiplied exceedingly." That phrase "were fruitful, and multiplied" is, in Hebrew, the very wording of God's first blessing on humanity in Genesis chapter 1. Not because they were cleverer — because the promise of God was on them. And the deepest question in this passage is in fact addressed to every single one of us: when the silver goes to zero, the livestock goes to zero and the land goes to zero, what is a person left with? The people said, "There is nothing left … but our bodies, and our lands." What a person is finally left holding is the One he has believed in.
4. Please Don't Bury Me in Egypt
The last section of this chapter is the heaviest thing in it.

"Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were one hundred forty-seven years. The time came near that Israel must die, and he called his son Joseph, and said to him, 'If now I have found favor in your sight, please put your hand under my thigh, and deal kindly and truly with me. Please don't bury me in Egypt, but when I sleep with my fathers, you shall carry me out of Egypt, and bury me in their burying place.'" (Genesis 47:28–30)

Seventeen years. Take note of that number. Genesis 37 opens by saying, "Joseph, being seventeen years old, was feeding the flock with his brothers." The father had the son for seventeen years; and the son, in the end, had the father for seventeen years.
Even a number like that, God squares up.
"Please put your hand under my thigh" is the most solemn form an oath can take — it is exactly how Abraham had his old servant swear back in chapter 24.
And what is it that he asks for? Not to be buried in Egypt.
Brothers and sisters, this matters enormously.

He is living in "the best of the land" of Egypt — "the best", a phrase Pharaoh himself used twice with his own mouth. His son is prime minister. He lacks nothing there in food or clothing, and his old age is a comfortable one.
And yet what he says is: do not leave me here.
He lived in the best of lands; his heart was in the land of the promise.

To let Jesus be King is to let him decide where I finally belong. You can make your money in a place, raise a family in a place, be blessed in a place — but that place does not get to decide where you belong.
And then comes the last sentence of the chapter: "Then Israel bowed himself on the bed's head." (Genesis 47:31) — and the Hebrew verb there, וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ (*vayishtachu*), is the verb for worship.
When Hebrews chapter 11 takes up this verse, it says, "By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff."
Leaning on the top of his staff.
That staff is the one that was in his hand when he fled at seventy-seven — the one he spoke of himself back in chapter 32: "for with just my staff I crossed over this Jordan."
And it is the same staff he leaned on for the rest of his life after he was left limping.
At the beginning of his life he ran away holding a staff; at the end of his life he worshipped leaning on the same staff.
A man who admits that "the days of the years of my life have been few and evil" — and the last picture we are given of him is this: worshipping, leaning on the top of his staff.
Those two things are not a contradiction. That is what real faith looks like.
He was living in "the best of the land" of Egypt. Why did he insist on not being buried there?

His son was prime minister; Pharaoh himself twice called it "the best" of the land; he lacked nothing there and his old age was a comfortable one. And yet what he says is: do not leave me here. He lived in the best of lands, but his heart was in the land of the promise. To let Jesus be King is to let him decide where I finally belong — you can make your money in a place, raise a family in a place and be blessed in a place, but that place does not get to decide where you belong. And there is one more number here that is deeply moving: he lived in Egypt seventeen years, exactly as long as the seventeen years he had had with Joseph before Joseph was sold away. Even a number like that, God squares up — the father had the son for seventeen years, and the son, in the end, had the father for seventeen years.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
There are several places in this chapter that are very easy to preach crooked.

The first distortion is to scold Jacob for saying "few and evil." God did not rebuke him, the narrator did not add one word of comment, and after he had said it he went straight on to bless Pharaoh. Scold that sentence and all you will produce is a congregation that pretends to be fine inside the church. The test is this: when they have heard you, do they dare to tell the truth more, or have they simply got better at putting on a face?

The second distortion is to use Joseph's land policy to prop up some particular economic argument. That is narrative, not norm; and the people came and asked for it themselves, and the rate left four fifths in their hands. Make it the basis of a policy and you have turned the pulpit into a political platform.

The third distortion is to preach "blessing Pharaoh" as though Christians were a cut above other people. Standing means the office of carrying a promise, not a superior status. Preach it as superiority and you will breed spiritual pride — which is precisely the thing this book has been dismantling all along.

The fourth distortion is to preach "living in the best of the land" as a guarantee that God will make his children prosperous. In this very same chapter, a whole nation sells its land and sells itself. The blessing of Goshen was given by God for the sake of his own plan; it is not a formula for getting rich.

The fifth distortion is to preach "don't bury me in Egypt" as though Christians ought not to love the place where they live. Jacob lived in Egypt for seventeen years, enjoyed what that land provided, and blessed that land's king. He is not ungrateful; he is simply not confused — gratitude and belonging are two different things.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: it is very hard for us to tell the truth inside a church. Somebody asks, "How have you been lately?" and we say, "All good, thank the Lord." What gets shared at the prayer meeting is usually a difficulty that has already been dealt with. The thing that is still actually bleeding — that we do not mention, because we are afraid of being told our faith is weak, and afraid it will be passed around. Brothers and sisters, Jacob stood in front of Pharaoh and said "few and evil", and God did not rebuke him. More than half of the Psalms are laments. So this week, please tell God the truth at least once: take the bitterest thing of this past year and say it to him directly, with no packaging, and without adding "but I believe God has a good purpose in it." That sentence can come later. He can take it.

The second question: we settle our hearts down very easily in some "best of the land." A house, a status, a school, a pension — none of these are bad things, and a great many of them are God's grace. But the moment the heart takes up residence there, we begin to measure everything by that place. Jacob lived in the best of lands and still gave the instruction: don't bury me here. So this week, please examine one thing: which single thing is your deepest sense of security resting on? If that one thing were taken away, would you still be standing?
7. Living 321 Out — Worshipping, Leaning on the Top of a Staff
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. "Then Israel bowed himself on the bed's head" — and Hebrews says that he "worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff." And the Lord Jesus, in the garden of Gethsemane, said, "My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death." He did not pretend that it was not bitter. And then he said, "nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire." My role model is this: he said the bitterness out loud, honestly, and then obeyed all the same.

The Bible is my standard. The standard is not "a Christian is not allowed to speak of bitterness"; the standard is "casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you." And to cast them on him, you first have to admit that they are worries.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. When to speak, whom to speak to, how far to go in the speaking — that needs guidance. Not every hard thing belongs in every setting. To rely on our intellect and lean on ourselves is to end up in worry — you will weigh and re-weigh what other people are going to think. To rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit is to end up in gladness — he will give you the right person and the right moment.

Let Jesus be King. "Please don't bury me in Egypt" — he refused to let the best of lands decide where he belonged. To let Jesus be King is to let him decide where I finally belong; and a person who is clear about where he belongs can live at ease in any place at all.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. Standing there in front of Pharaoh, he did not trade on his connections and he did not say, "My son is the prime minister." What he did was to bless — he carried the name of God into that court. Giving God the glory is not a matter of how beautifully we speak; it is that wherever we go, we take him with us.

Establish God's system. He blessed Pharaoh twice over. Our identity is not defined by our circumstances. To establish God's system is to walk into any room at all carrying the blessing God has given you — including the rooms where you feel you count for least.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Staff
We come and stand in front of Pharaoh with four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "On the whole my life has been rather a success." Jacob's answer was "few and evil." Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights — packaging even our own life into a presentable report card. Humility is returning to our originally intended position as human beings, and daring to say, "I have not attained to the days of my fathers." And it is the person who can say that sentence who is able to give a blessing.

The fearful heart says, "If I tell the truth, what will people think of me?" Pharaoh did not throw him out for saying that his years had been bitter, and God did not rebuke him either. That reaction you are afraid of will most likely never happen; and the people who genuinely care about you are precisely the ones who want to hear the truth.

The ashamed heart says, "I have made nothing of my life; what have I got that could bless anybody?" What is in your hands? All Jacob had in his hands was a staff and a promise. And that promise was what qualified him to bless Pharaoh. If you are in Christ, then you have something in your hands to give away.

The wounded heart says, "Few and evil — that is my whole life." Yes. That sentence is in the Bible, and the Bible did not delete it. But brothers and sisters, look at that last verse: the man who said that sentence ends up worshipping, leaning on the top of his staff. The bitterness is real, and the worship is real too. Both of those can live in the same person.
Four kinds of heart, one staff. And that staff is the evidence of a whole lifetime walked with a limp.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, towards God. Take the bitterest thing of this past year and tell him directly. No packaging, no explaining, no hurrying to add "but I believe …" Just say it all the way to the end.
Second, towards yourself. Write down three words to describe this year of yours, and then carry those three words into your prayer.
Third, towards other people. In some setting where you feel your standing is very small, bless one person. In the name of the Lord, and concretely.
Fourth, towards your daily living. Examine which one thing your deepest sense of security is resting on. Write it down, and then, in God's presence, put it back into his hands.
Fifth, towards your mission. Just as Jacob gave his instructions about a burying place, say once, clearly, where you finally belong — say it to God, and say it to your family.

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is an old man of a hundred and thirty in the Bible who, when a king asked him about his life, said it had been "few and evil." Second: having said how bitter it was, he blessed that king anyway, and at the very end he worshipped God leaning on his walking stick. Third: the God I believe in does not need me to put on a good performance before he will listen to me.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will tell God the truth; that I will call the bitter thing bitter, because he can take it.
I declare that even while I admit my own weakness, I will still bless other people.
I declare that the best of lands does not get to decide where I belong; I let Jesus decide where I finally belong.
I declare that I will spend my whole life worshipping, leaning on the top of my staff; because the bitterness is real, and God's faithfulness is more real still.
Being honest about the bitterness and still blessing people — how do you do both at once?

Two things are present in this passage at the same time: he admits his own bitterness, and he still blesses other people. That is a very mature life. An immature life can only pick one of the two: either pretend nothing is wrong and press the pain down, which turns sour in the end; or be swallowed by the pain and be no blessing to anybody. Honest on the one hand, giving on the other — this was the last lesson of Jacob's life, and he learned it. In practice you can train it like this: find one safe person and tell that person the truth; you do not have to say it to everybody. And in the places where you serve, go on giving out the blessing you are there to give — the place where you speak the truth and the place where you give the blessing are allowed to be two different places.
An old shepherd of a hundred and thirty, standing in Pharaoh's hall. There is no tribute in his hands, no army behind him, nothing at all he could offer in exchange. He has only a staff.

He blesses that king. He says that the days of his life have been few and evil. He gives instructions not to be buried in this best of lands. And at the last, he worships, leaning on the top of his staff.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on other people, not on our circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because the Lord who sweated as it were great drops of blood in Gethsemane, and who cried out from the cross, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?", is the same Lord who said, "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!" He said the bitterness out loud, honestly, and he obeyed completely, all the way to the end; and he walked that road so that people like us — people whose days have been few and evil — might at the last also worship, leaning on the top of a staff.

May God bless every one of us to dare to speak the truth in his presence; may our hearts, while we live in the best of lands, still be turned towards that land of promise; and may the last picture of our lives be worship. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson home as a clear mindset.

1. ★★★ Honest about the bitterness on the one hand, blessing people all the same on the other. Which side are you more likely to fall off — pretending nothing is wrong, or being swallowed by the pain?
2. ★★ Standing means the office of carrying a promise, not a superior status. How does that distinction apply to the way you serve?
3. ★ He said, "the years of my pilgrimage." How would seeing yourself as a traveller passing through change the way you look at what is in your hands?
4. ★★ He lived in the best of lands, but his heart was in the land of the promise. What decides where you belong?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (on the whole my life has been rather a success), fearful (will saying it was bitter make me look as though I have no faith?), ashamed (there is nothing much to show for my life), wounded (few and evil, that is my whole life). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "The days of the years of my life have been few and evil." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there some hard thing you have been wrapping up in spiritual language all this time? What is it that stops you from telling the truth about it?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "If somebody asked me how my life has gone, what I would really want to say is …"
9. ★★ This week, who will you tell the truth to once, and who will you bless once? Give two names.

Leader's reminder: this question will make people look back over a lifetime of losses. Do not round it off with "just give thanks to the Lord" — let the person finish first. If someone speaks of a long-standing hopelessness or of the grief of losing someone, stay with him privately after the meeting, and help him find professional support where that is needed.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, who most needs to hear a word of blessing? Say that sentence out loud now.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at your workplace, what is that "skill people look down on" of yours?

12. ★★★ The traveller's practice: this week, point out one thing you are gripping too tightly, and change the way you speak of it from "mine" to "what the Lord has entrusted to me to look after." Say now what it is.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and this week tell him one unvarnished truth. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is an old refugee of a hundred and thirty in the Bible who stood in front of the king of Egypt and opened his mouth to bless that monarch. Second: the king asked him how his life had gone, and he said, "The days of the years of my life have been few and evil" — and having said it, he blessed the king a second time. Third: so what I have learned is that a person can be honest about the bitterness and still have a blessing to give. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one hard thing you have never said out loud, and the person you are going to bless. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to make us people who can speak the truth in his presence and give out a blessing in the presence of others.
